Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Péter Magyar The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace Editorial As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.29 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.37 EDT Share S ome elections are more important than others. Since taking office in May, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has embarked upon the country’s most far-reaching and dramatic programme of transformation since the fall of communism in 1989. Mr Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán, established a soft autocracy which thrived on corruption and, over 16 years, exerted its grip on most areas of Hungarian life, from religion to culture and the media. It is being dismantled at extraordinary pace. Last week, a newly appointed president took office following the sacking of Tamás Sulyok, accused by Mr Magyar of having rubber-stamped the erosion of the rule of law in the country. In stark contrast, András Baka is a former president of Hungary’s supreme court, a role he was removed from by the Orbán regime in an action judged unlawful by the European court of human rights. On Hungary’s national day last Thursday, news bulletins returned to the main state television channel, having been shut down for six weeks. In July, viewers had encountered a blank screen along with the message: “Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long.” Ending naked bias on state TV was one of Mr Magyar’s key pledges, in a campaign that saw him buck an electoral system weighted in favour of Mr Orbán and win a landslide . The tempo has been equally relentless when it comes to attacking networks of corruption and clientelism built up over a decade and a half. Well over €100bn in public funds, including billions of euros of EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during the Orbán years. Investigators have been empowered to go after it via a new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Mr Magyar has also confirmed Hungarian participation in the European public prosecutor’s office, enabling the EU to better protect itself from financial crime in the country. It will take time for Hungary to feel like a normal pluralist European democracy again. For now, Mr Magyar is functioning as a one-man political whirlwind, heading what amounts to a national unity government elected by voters across the political spectrum. Concerns have been raised over constitutional manoeuvring to ensure many MPs in Mr Orbán’s Fidesz party cannot stand again, and Mr Baka has warned against appearing to take revenge on the former prime minister’s supporters. But a root-and-branch approach to de-Orbánising Hungary was what was needed, and continues to be rewarded by record levels of popularity in polls. The next major threshold is likely to be crossed in the autumn. Brussels has given Hungary’s new government until the end of this month to demonstrate that enough is being done on corruption to warrant the release of over €10bn in frozen funds. If, as seems likely, the vast majority of the funds are disbursed, it will seal the ongoing rapprochement between the EU and its former rogue member state. In May, Mr Magyar relocated the prime minister’s office away from a controversially cordoned-off former Carmelite monastery used by Mr Orbán, opening the building up to the public. “I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” he had told interviewers soon after taking power. Three months on, the symbolism is being supplemented by a peaceful political revolution. Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/EPA Xi Jinping Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen and agencies Mon 16 Nov 2026 08.51 EST Last modified on Mon 16 Nov 2026 09.14 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The unprecedented meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said. The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit , cements Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen. The topics up for discussion are far from clear but many – including the UN secretary general – are hoping that denuclearisation will be discussed between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said. China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items. “[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said the foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia , and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.” The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said on Monday that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. View image in fullscreen People gather to watch a light show on buildings in Shenzhen, the host city for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Photograph: Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty Images However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough. Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict, and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”. In contrast, as feared by Kyiv, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine might not come up at all, despite Putin reportedly wanting it to. US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up. For Xi, “much of the political benefit” will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion. Sari Arho Havrén, from the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X : “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host.
